hs_math_t11_st01.title: Perimeter and area of plane figures
hs_math_t11_st01.overview: Plane mensuration measures two different attributes of a flat figure: the length of its outside boundary and the amount of surface enclosed. The correct formula depends on the shape, and area formulas that use a height require a perpendicular height.

key_concepts.definition: The total length of the outside boundary.
key_concepts.details: Add the lengths of all outer sides. Perimeter is a one-dimensional measure, so its units are cm, m or another length unit. For a rectangle, P = 2(l + w); for a square, P = 4a. For a regular polygon with n equal sides of length a, P = na.

key_concepts.definition: The measure of the two-dimensional region enclosed by a boundary.
key_concepts.details: Area can be understood as the number of unit squares that cover a region without gaps or overlaps. It is measured in square units such as cm² or m². Rectangle: A = lw; square: A = a²; triangle: A = ½bh; parallelogram: A = bh; trapezium/trapezoid: A = ½(a+b)h, where a and b are the parallel sides.

key_concepts.concept: Area of a rhombus and kite
key_concepts.definition: Area determined by the lengths of the diagonals.
key_concepts.details: For a rhombus or kite whose diagonals are perpendicular, A = ½d₁d₂. The diagonals are the full lengths between opposite vertices, not half-diagonals.

key_concepts.definition: Use the measurement that is perpendicular to the selected base.
key_concepts.details: In a triangle or parallelogram, the height is the shortest perpendicular distance between the base line and the opposite vertex or parallel side. It may lie outside an obtuse triangle. A sloping side is not automatically the height.

key_concepts.definition: Perimeter is length; area is length multiplied by length.
key_concepts.details: If lengths are in metres, area is in m². Convert all lengths to one unit before substituting. For area conversions, square the linear conversion factor: 1 m² = 10,000 cm².

variables.h: perpendicular distance between the parallel sides

worked_examples.problem: A trapezium has parallel sides 10 cm and 16 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area.
solution_steps: Substitute a = 10 cm, b = 16 cm and h = 5 cm.

worked_examples.problem: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7.5 m wide. Find the fencing length and the area.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a sloping side as the height of a triangle or parallelogram.
common_mistakes.correction: Draw or identify a perpendicular line to the base. Use that perpendicular distance as h.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing perimeter units with area units.
common_mistakes.correction: Write length answers in units such as cm and area answers in square units such as cm².

common_mistakes.mistake: Converting m² to cm² using a factor of 100 only.
common_mistakes.correction: Square the linear factor: 1 m² = (100 cm)² = 10,000 cm².

quick_summary: Perimeter measures the outer boundary; area measures the enclosed surface.
Use perpendicular height in triangle, parallelogram and trapezium formulas.
For a regular n-sided polygon, perimeter = n × side length.
Area units are squared; convert squared units by squaring the length conversion factor.

hs_math_t11_st02.title: Area of composite shapes
hs_math_t11_st02.overview: A composite plane figure is formed by combining two or more familiar shapes or by removing a smaller region from a larger one. Its area can be found by partitioning it into simple shapes or subtracting cut-outs. Perimeter must be treated separately because only exposed boundary segments count.

key_concepts.definition: Split a complex figure into non-overlapping familiar parts.
key_concepts.details: Draw construction lines to make rectangles, triangles, trapezia, semicircles or other known shapes. Find each part's area and add. Check that the parts cover the required region exactly once.

key_concepts.definition: Subtract missing regions from a simple enclosing shape.
key_concepts.details: Enclose the figure in a rectangle or another familiar shape. Calculate the enclosing area, calculate the cut-out area, and subtract: required area = whole area − removed area.

key_concepts.definition: Use the total lengths to determine smaller lengths.
key_concepts.details: When a shape is split, a remaining segment may be the difference between an overall length and a known part. For example, if a total width is 12 m and one section is 4 m, the remaining width is 8 m.

key_concepts.definition: Add only the lengths on the outside boundary.
key_concepts.details: Internal partition lines are not part of the perimeter. Trace the outside edge once. For an L-shape, derive missing outer lengths from aligned horizontal and vertical totals.

worked_examples.problem: An L-shaped floor is made from a 10 m × 8 m rectangle with a 4 m × 3 m corner removed. Find its area.
solution_steps: Area of the full rectangle = 10×8 = 80 m².
Area of the removed rectangle = 4×3 = 12 m².

worked_examples.problem: A shape consists of a 9 cm × 4 cm rectangle and a right triangle with base 4 cm and height 3 cm attached along a 4 cm side. Find the total area.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding the area of an overlapping part twice.
common_mistakes.correction: Choose non-overlapping pieces or subtract the overlap once.

common_mistakes.mistake: Including an internal dividing line in the perimeter.
common_mistakes.correction: Trace only the exposed outside boundary; partition lines are not perimeter.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using an original total length for a smaller partition without recalculating it.
common_mistakes.correction: Subtract the known section from the overall length to find the remaining dimension.

quick_summary: Break composite figures into familiar non-overlapping shapes, or subtract cut-outs from an enclosing shape.
Calculate missing dimensions before applying formulas.
Area is combined by addition/subtraction; perimeter includes only the exposed outside edges.

hs_math_t11_st03.title: Circumference and area of circles
hs_math_t11_st03.overview: A circle is the set of points in a plane at a fixed distance from a centre. Its radius, diameter, circumference and area are related by the constant π. Use the radius in the area formula and distinguish exact answers involving π from decimal approximations.

key_concepts.definition: The radius joins the centre to the circle; the diameter passes through the centre.
key_concepts.details: The diameter is twice the radius: d = 2r. A diameter is the longest chord of a circle.

key_concepts.definition: The length of the complete circular boundary.
key_concepts.details: The ratio of circumference to diameter is the constant π. Thus C = πd = 2πr. Circumference is a length and is measured in linear units.

key_concepts.definition: The measure of the region enclosed by the circumference.
key_concepts.details: A = πr². The radius must be squared. If the diameter is given, first calculate r = d/2.

key_concepts.definition: Find a missing radius or diameter from circumference or area.
key_concepts.details: From C = 2πr, r = C/(2π). From A = πr², r = √(A/π). A radius is positive, so take the positive square root.

key_concepts.definition: A semicircle is half a disk; an annulus is the region between two concentric circles.
key_concepts.details: Semicircle area = ½πr². The perimeter of a semicircular region includes the curved half-circumference plus the diameter: P = πr+2r. An annulus has area π(R²−r²), where R is the outer radius and r the inner radius.

worked_examples.problem: A circular pond has radius 7 m. Find its circumference and area in terms of π and using π = 22/7.
worked_examples.final_answer: Circumference = 14π m = 44 m; area = 49π m² = 154 m²

worked_examples.problem: A circular plate has area 154 cm². Find its radius using π = 22/7.

common_mistakes.mistake: Substituting the diameter directly into A = πr².
common_mistakes.correction: If diameter d is given, use r = d/2 before calculating area.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving the semicircle's curved arc as its full perimeter.
common_mistakes.correction: Add the straight diameter: P = πr+2r.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding π too early when an exact answer is requested.
common_mistakes.correction: Keep answers in terms of π until a decimal approximation is specifically required.

quick_summary: C = πd = 2πr; A = πr².
Diameter = 2 × radius.
For a semicircular region, perimeter includes the diameter.
For an annulus, subtract the inner circle's area from the outer circle's area.

hs_math_t11_st04.title: Arc length and sector area
hs_math_t11_st04.overview: A sector is a region bounded by two radii and an arc. The arc length and sector area are the same fraction of the full circumference and area as the central angle is of one complete revolution. Degree formulas use 360°, while radian formulas require the angle in radians.

key_concepts.concept: Central angle and fraction of a circle
key_concepts.definition: The central angle determines the fraction of the full circle represented by a sector.
key_concepts.details: For θ degrees, the fraction is θ/360. A 90° sector is one quarter of a circle; a 180° sector is a semicircle.

key_concepts.definition: The length of the curved part of the sector boundary.
key_concepts.details: For degrees, L = (θ/360)×2πr. For radians, L = rθ. Arc length is a linear measurement.

key_concepts.definition: The area enclosed by two radii and the included arc.
key_concepts.details: For degrees, A = (θ/360)×πr². For radians, A = ½r²θ. Sector area is measured in square units.

key_concepts.definition: The total boundary length of the sector.
key_concepts.details: The perimeter includes the arc and both radii: P = L+2r. Do not confuse it with arc length alone.

key_concepts.definition: Two ways of measuring angles.
key_concepts.details: A full turn is 360° or 2π radians. Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by π/180. Use the radian formulas only when θ is expressed in radians.

worked_examples.problem: A sector has radius 7 cm and central angle 90°. Find its arc length, area and perimeter using π = 22/7.
worked_examples.final_answer: Arc length = 11 cm; area = 38.5 cm²; perimeter = 25 cm

worked_examples.problem: An arc is 6π cm long and subtends an angle of π/2 radians. Find the radius.
solution_steps: Use the radian formula L = rθ.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a degree value in a radian formula or vice versa.
common_mistakes.correction: Check the angle unit first. Convert degrees to radians when using L = rθ or A = ½r²θ.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling arc length the sector perimeter.
common_mistakes.correction: Add both radii to the arc: P = L+2r.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using θ/360 when θ is in radians.
common_mistakes.correction: The denominator 360 applies only to degrees; use the radian formulas for radians.

quick_summary: Arc length is the corresponding fraction of the circumference.
Sector area is the same fraction of the circle's area.
For radians, L = rθ and A = ½r²θ.
Sector perimeter = arc length + two radii.

hs_math_t11_st05.title: Surface area of prisms
hs_math_t11_st05.overview: A prism has two congruent, parallel bases and a constant cross-section along its length. Its surface area is the sum of its base faces and lateral faces. A net makes the faces visible and helps distinguish lateral surface area from total surface area.

key_concepts.definition: A prism has two matching parallel bases connected by parallelogram faces.
key_concepts.details: In a right prism, the lateral faces are rectangles. The length of the prism is the perpendicular distance between its bases. A cuboid and cube are special prisms.

key_concepts.definition: The combined area of the side faces, excluding the two bases.
key_concepts.details: For a right prism, LSA = perimeter of base × prism length. If the base perimeter is P and prism length is h, LSA = Ph.

key_concepts.definition: The area of every external face, including both bases.
key_concepts.details: TSA = Ph+2B for a right prism, where B is the area of one base. For a cuboid this becomes 2(lw+lh+wh); for a cube it is 6a².

key_concepts.definition: Count only the faces that are actually present or exposed.
key_concepts.details: An open-top box has one base and its lateral faces, so its area is Ph+B. If both ends are open, only the lateral faces are counted. For painting or wrapping, exclude hidden or absent faces.

key_concepts.definition: A net is a flat arrangement of all faces that folds into the solid.
key_concepts.details: The net of a prism contains two congruent base shapes and one rectangle for each side of the base. The rectangle widths correspond to the base side lengths and their common height is the prism length.

A cuboid measures 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm. Find its total surface area.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the area of a base as the lateral surface area.
common_mistakes.correction: For a right prism, multiply the base perimeter by the prism length: LSA = Ph.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting one or both bases in total surface area.
common_mistakes.correction: TSA includes all external faces; add 2B for a closed prism.

common_mistakes.mistake: Counting an absent lid or an internal joining face.
common_mistakes.correction: Read whether the prism is open, closed or joined to another solid and count only exposed faces.

quick_summary: For a right prism, LSA = base perimeter × prism length.
TSA = LSA + areas of both bases.
A net displays all faces and helps prevent omissions.
Open prisms require only the areas of faces that exist and are exposed.

hs_math_t11_st06.title: Volume of prisms
hs_math_t11_st06.overview: The volume of a prism is the area of its constant cross-section multiplied by the perpendicular distance between its two congruent bases. This rule works for triangular, rectangular, trapezoidal and other prisms. The cross-sectional area and prism length must use compatible units.

key_concepts.definition: Every slice parallel to the bases has the same shape and area.
key_concepts.details: This property allows a prism to be viewed as identical layers stacked along its length. The area of one base is often written B or A.

key_concepts.definition: Multiply the base or cross-sectional area by the prism length.
key_concepts.details: V = Bh. For a triangular prism, B = ½b×h_triangle; multiply this area by the prism length. Do not confuse the triangle's perpendicular height with the prism's length.

key_concepts.definition: Volume measures three-dimensional space.
key_concepts.details: If dimensions are in centimetres, volume is in cm³. If the base area is in m² and prism length in m, volume is in m³.

key_concepts.definition: Capacity is the amount a container can hold.
key_concepts.details: For water or other liquids, use internal dimensions. 1 cm³ = 1 mL, 1000 cm³ = 1 L and 1 m³ = 1000 L.

variables.h: perpendicular distance between the bases / prism length

worked_examples.problem: A triangular prism has a triangular cross-section with base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. Its length is 12 cm. Find its volume.
solution_steps: Area of triangular cross-section B = ½×6×4 = 12 cm².

worked_examples.problem: A prism has a cross-sectional area of 35 cm² and volume 420 cm³. Find its length.
solution_steps: Use V = Bh, so h = V/B.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the triangle's height as the prism length.
common_mistakes.correction: The triangle's height is used to calculate B; multiply B by the separate prism length.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using inconsistent units.
common_mistakes.correction: Convert all dimensions to one length unit before calculating the base area and volume.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing volume in square units.
common_mistakes.correction: Volume is measured in cubic units such as cm³ or m³.

quick_summary: The volume of every prism is V = base area × perpendicular length.
Find the cross-sectional area first, then multiply by the prism length.
Use internal dimensions for container capacity.
Volume uses cubic units.

hs_math_t11_st07.title: Cylinders
hs_math_t11_st07.overview: A right circular cylinder has two equal, parallel circular bases joined by a curved surface. When the curved surface is cut along a vertical line and unrolled, it forms a rectangle whose dimensions are the circumference of the base and the cylinder's height. This explains the curved-surface-area formula.

key_concepts.definition: A cylinder is described by its radius r and perpendicular height h.
key_concepts.details: The radius is measured from the centre of a circular base to its edge. The diameter is 2r. The height is the perpendicular distance between the circular bases.

key_concepts.definition: The area of the curved wall only.
key_concepts.details: Unrolling the curved wall gives a rectangle of width 2πr and height h. Therefore CSA = 2πrh.

key_concepts.definition: The curved wall plus the two circular ends.
key_concepts.details: For a closed cylinder, TSA = 2πrh+2πr² = 2πr(h+r). For an open-top cylinder, include only one circular base: area = 2πrh+πr².

key_concepts.definition: The area of a circular base multiplied by the height.
key_concepts.details: V = πr²h. Use the internal radius and internal height when calculating a tank's capacity.

key_concepts.definition: The inner and outer radii may both matter.
key_concepts.details: For a hollow cylindrical wall, the material's cross-sectional area is π(R²−r²), where R is the outer radius and r is the inner radius. For a pipe of length h, material volume = π(R²−r²)h. Identify whether the problem asks for the material or the space inside.

worked_examples.final_answer: CSA = 48π cm²; TSA = 66π cm²; volume = 72π cm³

worked_examples.problem: A cylindrical tank has internal radius 20 cm and height 60 cm. Find its capacity in litres using π = 3.14.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using diameter as the radius.
common_mistakes.correction: If diameter is given, divide it by 2 before substituting.

common_mistakes.mistake: Including two circular bases for an open-top cylinder.
common_mistakes.correction: Count only the bases that are present and exposed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using external dimensions for tank capacity.
common_mistakes.correction: Use internal dimensions because the liquid occupies the inside space.

quick_summary: CSA = 2πrh; it is the rectangle formed by unrolling the curved wall.
A closed cylinder has TSA = 2πrh+2πr².
Volume = πr²h.
For hollow cylinders, distinguish material volume from internal capacity.

hs_math_t11_st08.title: Cones
hs_math_t11_st08.overview: A right circular cone has one circular base and a curved surface that narrows to an apex. Its volume is one-third of the volume of a cylinder with the same base radius and vertical height. Surface-area calculations use the slant height, while volume uses the perpendicular vertical height.

key_concepts.definition: A cone has a base radius, vertical height and slant height.
key_concepts.details: The vertical height h is perpendicular to the base and joins the apex to the centre of the base. The slant height l runs along the sloping surface from the apex to the base rim.

key_concepts.definition: A central cross-section forms a right triangle.
key_concepts.details: For a right circular cone, l² = h²+r². Thus l = √(h²+r²). The radius, vertical height and slant height are not interchangeable.

key_concepts.definition: The curved surface is the cone's lateral covering; total area also includes its circular base.
key_concepts.details: CSA = πrl. TSA = πrl+πr² = πr(l+r). The curved surface unrolls into a sector of a circle.

key_concepts.definition: The cone holds one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.
key_concepts.details: V = ⅓πr²h. The vertical height, not the slant height, is used.

formulas.name: Cone curved and total surface area

worked_examples.final_answer: Slant height = 5 cm; CSA = 47.1 cm²; volume = 37.68 cm³

worked_examples.problem: A cone has radius 7 cm and slant height 10 cm. Find its total surface area in terms of π.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using slant height in the volume formula.
common_mistakes.correction: Volume uses vertical height h; use Pythagoras if h is not given.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using vertical height in the curved-area formula.
common_mistakes.correction: Cone CSA uses slant height l.

common_mistakes.mistake: Omitting the circular base when total surface area is requested.
common_mistakes.correction: Add πr² to the curved surface area for a closed solid cone.

quick_summary: Volume uses vertical height: V = ⅓πr²h.
Curved surface area uses slant height: CSA = πrl.
TSA of a solid cone = πrl+πr².
For a right cone, l² = h²+r².

hs_math_t11_st09.title: Spheres and hemispheres
hs_math_t11_st09.overview: A sphere is a three-dimensional surface whose points are all at the same distance from its centre. A hemisphere is half of a sphere. The flat circular face created by cutting a sphere through its centre must be included when total surface area of a solid hemisphere is requested.

key_concepts.definition: The area of the entire curved outer surface of a sphere.
key_concepts.details: A sphere has no flat faces, edges or vertices. Its surface area is 4πr².

key_concepts.definition: The space enclosed by the sphere.
key_concepts.details: V = 4/3πr³. The radius is cubed, so volume is measured in cubic units.

key_concepts.definition: A hemisphere is exactly half of a sphere.
key_concepts.details: Its volume is 2/3πr³ and its curved surface area is 2πr².

key_concepts.definition: The curved dome plus its flat circular base.
key_concepts.details: For a solid hemisphere, TSA = 2πr²+πr² = 3πr². For an open bowl or hollow hemisphere where the flat base is absent, the curved area alone may be required.

key_concepts.definition: Two hemispheres of the same radius can form a sphere.
key_concepts.details: When two hemispheres are joined along their circular bases, the joining faces are internal and are not included in the external surface area.

visual_aids.title: Sphere and hemisphere surfaces
visual_aids.caption: A solid hemisphere has a curved dome and one flat circular base.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using 2πr² as the total surface area of a solid hemisphere.
common_mistakes.correction: 2πr² is only the curved surface area. Add the flat base πr² to get 3πr².

common_mistakes.mistake: Using r² instead of r³ in sphere volume.
common_mistakes.correction: Volume is three-dimensional and uses r cubed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Counting the circular joining face of two joined hemispheres.
common_mistakes.correction: The joining face is internal; include only exposed outer surfaces.

quick_summary: Sphere SA = 4πr² and volume = 4/3πr³.
Hemisphere volume is half the sphere volume.
Hemisphere CSA = 2πr²; solid hemisphere TSA = 3πr².
Always identify whether a flat base is present and exposed.

hs_math_t11_st10.title: Pyramids
hs_math_t11_st10.overview: A pyramid has one polygonal base and triangular side faces that meet at a common apex. A regular pyramid has a regular polygon as its base and the apex vertically above the base centre. Its volume uses perpendicular height, while the lateral surface area of a regular pyramid uses the slant height of its triangular faces.

key_concepts.definition: A pyramid has a base, triangular lateral faces, edges and an apex.
key_concepts.details: The perpendicular height h is the shortest distance from the apex to the base plane. The slant height l of a regular pyramid is measured along the altitude of a triangular side face from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge.

key_concepts.definition: A pyramid has one-third the volume of a prism with the same base area and perpendicular height.
key_concepts.details: V = ⅓Bh, where B is the base area. The formula applies to pyramids with different polygonal bases.

key_concepts.concept: Lateral surface area of a regular pyramid
key_concepts.definition: The sum of the areas of its triangular side faces.
key_concepts.details: For a regular pyramid, LSA = ½Pl, where P is the base perimeter and l is the slant height. For a non-regular pyramid, calculate each triangular face area and add them.

key_concepts.definition: The lateral area plus the base area.
key_concepts.details: TSA = LSA+B. If the base is open or attached to another solid, include only the faces that are exposed.

key_concepts.definition: A useful special case.
key_concepts.details: For a square base of side a, B = a² and P = 4a. Therefore V = ⅓a²h, LSA = 2al and TSA = a²+2al. In a regular square pyramid, l² = h²+(a/2)².

formulas.name: Regular pyramid lateral and total surface area

variables.l: slant height of a triangular face

common_mistakes.mistake: Using slant height in the volume formula.
common_mistakes.correction: Pyramid volume uses perpendicular height from the apex to the base plane.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the slant height of one face as the height of every triangular face in an irregular pyramid.
common_mistakes.correction: For a non-regular pyramid, calculate each face with its own perpendicular face height.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the base in total surface area.
common_mistakes.correction: Add the base area if the base is part of the exposed solid surface.

quick_summary: Pyramid volume = ⅓ × base area × perpendicular height.
For a regular pyramid, LSA = ½ × base perimeter × face slant height.
TSA = LSA + base area.
Do not confuse vertical height with face slant height.

hs_math_t11_st11.title: Frustums — introduction
hs_math_t11_st11.overview: A frustum is the portion of a cone or pyramid left after its top is cut off by a plane parallel to the base. It has two parallel, similar bases of different sizes. This introductory lesson focuses on identifying dimensions and using standard formulas without lengthy derivations.

key_concepts.definition: A frustum has a larger lower base and a smaller upper base.
key_concepts.details: For a conical frustum, denote the larger and smaller radii by R and r. The vertical height is h and the slant height of the curved side is s. The two circular bases are parallel.

key_concepts.definition: The space inside the truncated cone.
key_concepts.details: V = ⅓πh(R²+r²+Rr). Both radii are needed. The height h is perpendicular to the circular bases.

key_concepts.definition: The curved band between the two circular rims.
key_concepts.details: CSA = π(R+r)s. For a closed frustum, total surface area also includes both circular ends: TSA = π(R+r)s+πR²+πr².

key_concepts.definition: The sloping distance between corresponding points on the two circular rims.
key_concepts.details: In a right circular frustum, the vertical height h and radial difference R−r form the legs of a right triangle: s = √(h²+(R−r)²).

key_concepts.definition: A parallel cut through a pyramid produces two similar polygonal bases.
key_concepts.details: For a regular pyramid frustum, volume is V = h/3(B₁+B₂+√(B₁B₂)), where B₁ and B₂ are the areas of the parallel bases. Its lateral area is ½(P₁+P₂)s for a right regular frustum, with corresponding base perimeters P₁ and P₂.

formulas.name: Conical frustum curved and total surface area
Regular pyramid frustum lateral surface area

variables.P₁, P₂: perimeters of the two parallel bases
variables.s: slant height of the trapezoidal lateral faces

formulas.name: Regular pyramid frustum total surface area

variables.P₁, P₂: perimeters of the two parallel bases
variables.B₁, B₂: areas of the two parallel bases

common_mistakes.mistake: Using R+r instead of R−r in the slant-height calculation.
common_mistakes.correction: The right triangle's horizontal leg is the difference of the radii, R−r.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using slant height in the volume formula.
common_mistakes.correction: The frustum volume formula uses vertical height h.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving out one circular end when total surface area of a closed frustum is requested.
common_mistakes.correction: Add both base areas πR² and πr² to the curved area.

quick_summary: A frustum is formed by cutting a cone or pyramid parallel to its base.
For a conical frustum, identify R, r, vertical height h and slant height s.
Use vertical height for volume and slant height for curved surface area.
For a closed conical frustum, TSA includes both circular ends.

hs_math_t11_st12.title: Composite three-dimensional solids
hs_math_t11_st12.overview: A composite solid is made by joining two or more simple solids or by removing part of a solid. Volume is usually found by adding or subtracting component volumes. Surface area requires identifying only the surfaces exposed on the outside; faces joined internally are not counted.

key_concepts.definition: Add the volumes of non-overlapping components.
key_concepts.details: If solids are joined without overlapping volume, V_total = V₁+V₂+…. Ensure that shared interfaces do not represent extra material.

key_concepts.concept: Volume of removed parts and hollow solids
key_concepts.definition: Subtract the volume of holes or cavities from the original solid.
key_concepts.details: For a drilled cylindrical hole, subtract πr²h from the original volume. For a hollow object, distinguish the material volume from the internal capacity.

key_concepts.definition: Count only faces exposed to the outside.
key_concepts.details: When two solids are joined along a face, the touching faces become internal and must be excluded. Calculate the exposed curved and flat surfaces separately.

key_concepts.definition: A hole can reduce volume while creating additional exposed surface.
key_concepts.details: A drilled tunnel contributes a new internal curved surface to the object's total boundary. Whether this surface is included depends on whether the question asks for all exposed material surface.

key_concepts.definition: Draw, label and separate the solid into familiar components.
key_concepts.details: Identify each component, list the dimensions, mark hidden joining faces, calculate component volumes or exposed surface areas, and combine the results with the correct operation.

variables.SA_external: Sum of areas of faces on the external boundary only

solution_steps: Exposed surfaces: hemisphere curved area, cylinder curved area and cylinder bottom.

worked_examples.problem: A cuboid measuring 10 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm has a cylindrical hole of radius 2 cm drilled completely through its 6 cm depth. Find the remaining volume in terms of π.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding the total surface areas of joined solids without adjustment.
common_mistakes.correction: Remove the joining faces from the total because they are hidden inside the composite object.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding the volume of a hole instead of subtracting it.
common_mistakes.correction: A hole is removed material; subtract its volume from the original solid.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming surface area always decreases when a hole is drilled.
common_mistakes.correction: A tunnel creates new internal curved surface, so total exposed boundary area may increase.

quick_summary: Add component volumes for joined solids; subtract cavities and holes.
For surface area, count only externally exposed faces.
Internal joining faces are not part of the outside surface.
A hole may reduce volume but add a new internal surface.

hs_math_t11_st13.title: Similar solids and scale factors
hs_math_t11_st13.overview: Similar solids have the same shape but may have different sizes. Corresponding linear dimensions are in a constant ratio k. Surface areas scale by the square of this ratio and volumes scale by its cube. These relationships allow unknown dimensions, areas or volumes to be found without repeating every measurement.

key_concepts.definition: Two solids are similar when their corresponding lengths are proportional and their corresponding angles match.
key_concepts.details: One solid can be enlarged or reduced uniformly to obtain the other. The ratio of corresponding lengths is the linear scale factor k.

key_concepts.definition: The ratio between corresponding lengths.
key_concepts.details: If a corresponding edge changes from 4 cm to 10 cm, k = 10/4 = 2.5 from the smaller solid to the larger one. State clearly which direction the scale factor describes.

key_concepts.definition: Areas depend on two dimensions.
key_concepts.details: If the linear scale factor is k, the surface-area scale factor is k². Thus A₂ = k²A₁ for corresponding total or corresponding surface areas.

key_concepts.definition: Volumes depend on three dimensions.
key_concepts.details: The volume scale factor is k³. Thus V₂ = k³V₁. Doubling every length multiplies surface area by 4 and volume by 8.

key_concepts.definition: Recover a length scale factor from area or volume information.
key_concepts.details: If the area ratio is q, the positive linear scale factor is √q. If the volume ratio is q, the positive linear scale factor is ∛q. Then use k to determine corresponding lengths.

formulas.name: Linear scale factor
formulas.equation: $$k=\frac{\text{corresponding length in solid 2}}{\text{corresponding length in solid 1}}$$

visual_aids.title: Linear, area and volume scale factors
visual_aids.caption: When all lengths are multiplied by k, area is multiplied by k² and volume by k³.

worked_examples.problem: Two similar cubes have corresponding edge lengths 3 cm and 6 cm. If the smaller cube has volume 27 cm³, find the larger cube's volume.
Two similar solids have surface areas in the ratio 25:49. Find the ratio of their corresponding lengths and their volume ratio.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using k instead of k² for surface area or k³ for volume.
common_mistakes.correction: Remember that area has two dimensions and volume has three.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reversing the scale factor.
common_mistakes.correction: Define the direction of comparison before calculating k; larger-to-smaller and smaller-to-larger are reciprocals.

common_mistakes.mistake: Taking a negative square or cube root for a physical scale factor.
common_mistakes.correction: A scale factor between lengths is positive; use the positive root.

quick_summary: Similar solids have proportional corresponding lengths.
Length ratio = k; surface-area ratio = k²; volume ratio = k³.
Double lengths means four times the area and eight times the volume.
Use square roots or cube roots to recover a linear scale factor from area or volume ratios.

hs_math_t11_st14.title: Applications of mensuration
hs_math_t11_st14.overview: Mensuration is used to estimate materials, costs, storage capacities and dimensions in practical situations. The key skill is translating the wording of a problem into the correct geometric quantity, choosing the relevant exposed surfaces or internal dimensions, converting units and interpreting the result.

key_concepts.definition: Identify whether the task concerns a boundary, covering or capacity.
key_concepts.details: Fencing, edging and borders require perimeter. Painting, tiling and wrapping require surface area. Filling, pouring and excavation require volume. A practical question may require more than one of these.

key_concepts.definition: Calculate the required area or volume before applying a rate.
key_concepts.details: For tiles, number required = floor area ÷ area of one tile; round up to a whole tile and allow for wastage if the problem specifies it. For paint or sheet material, use the relevant exposed surface area and subtract doors, windows or openings where appropriate.

key_concepts.definition: The space available inside a container determines its capacity.
key_concepts.details: Use internal dimensions for tanks and containers. Convert cubic centimetres to litres using 1000 cm³ = 1 L, and cubic metres to litres using 1 m³ = 1000 L.

key_concepts.definition: Length, area and volume conversions use different powers.
key_concepts.details: If 1 m = 100 cm, then 1 m² = 10,000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³. Convert all dimensions to compatible units before calculating.

key_concepts.definition: A numerical answer must match the requested quantity and its unit.
key_concepts.details: A number of tiles must be a whole number, a cost must be expressed in currency, and a capacity must be in units such as litres. Check whether the question asks for internal or external dimensions, open or closed surfaces, and whether wastage is included.

variables.N: number of tiles; round up if a fraction is needed

worked_examples.problem: A room is 8 m long and 6 m wide. It is tiled with square tiles of side 40 cm. Find the number of tiles required, ignoring wastage.
A cylindrical tank has internal radius 0.5 m and internal height 2 m. Find its capacity in litres using π = 3.14.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using volume when the question asks how much paint or tile is needed.
common_mistakes.correction: Painting and tiling normally require surface area; filling requires volume.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to convert tile dimensions into the same unit as the floor.
common_mistakes.correction: Convert all lengths to one unit before calculating area.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using external dimensions to estimate tank capacity.
common_mistakes.correction: Use internal dimensions because capacity is the volume of the space inside.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding a tile count down when a fraction remains.
common_mistakes.correction: A fraction of a tile still requires another tile; round up unless the problem specifies another arrangement.

quick_summary: Fencing uses perimeter; painting and tiling use surface area; filling uses volume.
Use internal dimensions for capacity and exposed surfaces for material estimates.
Square length-conversion factors for area and cube them for volume.
Interpret the answer and round appropriately for the real-world task.
